title: Robinhood
seoTitle: Design a Stock Trading App Like Robinhood
description: Design Robinhood — live stock prices, placing and cancelling orders through an exchange, and tracking order status — with real-time price fan-out and reliable order handling.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is Robinhood?
blocks.text: Robinhood is a commission-free brokerage app. Users watch live stock prices and place buy and sell orders, which Robinhood routes to an exchange for execution.

items: Users should see live prices for stocks they're viewing.
Users should be able to place market and limit orders to buy or sell.
Users should be able to cancel an order that hasn't been filled.
Users should be able to view the status of their orders.
Options, crypto and margin trading.
Portfolio analytics and charts.
Building our own matching engine — we route orders to an external exchange.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Order handling must be strongly consistent and never lose or duplicate an order.
Prices should update in near real time (< 1s) for viewers.
The system should scale to 20M daily users and handle market-open spikes.
Order placement should be low latency (< 200ms to acknowledgement).
Regulatory reporting.
Fraud detection.

blocks.text: Two very different flows: **prices** (massive one-to-many fan-out, where staleness of a second is fine) and **orders** (low volume per user but must be exactly right). We'll keep them separate.

items: **Symbol**: a tradable stock with its latest price.
**Order**: userId, symbol, side (buy/sell), type (market/limit), quantity, limit price, status, external exchange order ID.
**User**: the account placing orders.

blocks.code:
GET  /symbols/:symbol -> Symbol
GET  /prices/stream?symbols=AAPL,TSLA   (SSE)

POST /orders
{ "symbol": "AAPL", "side": "BUY", "type": "LIMIT", "quantity": 10, "limitPrice": 190.5 } -> Order

DELETE /orders/:orderId
GET    /orders?status&cursor -> Order[]

blocks.text: Robinhood consumes a market-data feed from exchanges or a data vendor. A **Price Ingest** service processes ticks and keeps the latest price per symbol. Clients subscribe to the symbols on screen.
2) Users should be able to place orders

An **Order Service** validates the order (buying power, market hours), writes it to the database as `PENDING`, and submits it to the exchange through an **Exchange Gateway** that speaks the exchange protocol (e.g. FIX).
3) Users should be able to cancel orders
Cancelling sends a cancel request to the exchange for the order's external ID. The order is only marked `CANCELLED` once the exchange confirms — it may have already filled.
4) Users should be able to view order status
The exchange sends execution reports (filled, partially filled, rejected, cancelled) back through the gateway; the Order Service updates the order status, and the client reads it.
1) How do we fan out prices to millions of viewers?

approach.text: Each client calls `GET /symbols/:symbol` every second for every symbol on screen.

challenges.text: Millions of users × several symbols × 1 request/sec is huge, wasteful load — and it spikes exactly at market open.

blocks.title: SSE with per-symbol pub/sub and coalescing

approach.text: Clients open one SSE connection listing their symbols. Each Price Stream server subscribes to only the symbols its connected clients need (Redis Pub/Sub or a similar fan-out layer) and pushes updates. Ticks are **coalesced** — at most a few updates per second per symbol are forwarded, since humans can't read faster and a fresher price replaces a stale one anyway.

challenges.text: Connections are long-lived, so servers must be scaled on connection count, and clients need to re-subscribe after reconnecting.

blocks.text: 2) How do we make sure orders are never lost or duplicated?

blocks.title: Submit to the exchange, then write to the database

approach.text: Send the order to the exchange first and save it after the response.

challenges.text: If we crash between the two, a real trade exists that we have no record of — unacceptable for a brokerage.

blocks.title: Write-ahead order record + client order IDs + reconciliation

items: Persist the order as `PENDING_SUBMIT` with a unique **client order ID** before contacting the exchange.
Submit to the exchange using that client order ID — exchanges reject duplicate IDs, so retries are safe.
Update to `SUBMITTED` with the exchange's ID, then apply execution reports as they arrive.
A **reconciliation job** periodically compares orders stuck in intermediate states with the exchange's view and repairs them.

approach.text: The API itself accepts an idempotency key so a user's double tap doesn't create two orders.

challenges.text: Order status is a state machine with many transitions; every transition must be applied idempotently because execution reports can be redelivered.

blocks.title: Pattern: Multi-step Processes
blocks.text: Placing an order spans our database and an external exchange. Durable state, idempotent steps and reconciliation are how you make a multi-step process reliable.
3) How do we survive market-open spikes?

Order requests are buffered behind the Order Service with per-user ordering preserved (partitioned by userId), and the Exchange Gateway enforces the exchange's rate limits. Price streaming scales horizontally on connection count and is pre-warmed before the opening bell, since the spike is entirely predictable.

quiz.question: Why persist the order before sending it to the exchange?
options: So a crash can never leave a real trade with no record
quiz.explanation: A write-ahead record plus reconciliation means every submitted order is accounted for.

quiz.question: What makes retrying an order submission to the exchange safe?
options: A unique client order ID the exchange deduplicates on
quiz.explanation: The exchange rejects a second order with the same client order ID.

quiz.question: Why coalesce price ticks before pushing them to clients?
options: Humans can't read faster, and the newest price replaces older ones
quiz.explanation: Forwarding a few updates per second per symbol cuts fan-out load with no visible loss.

quiz.question: When should an order be marked CANCELLED?
options: As soon as the user taps cancel
Only after the exchange confirms the cancel
quiz.explanation: The order may already have filled; the exchange is the source of truth.
